text: One yellow stripe on a bomb means it's live.
So why do some bombs have two?
In nineteen sixty-seven, a fire broke out on the carrier U S S Forrestal. A bomb in the flames exploded about a minute and a half later.
After that, the Navy pushed for bombs that could sit in a fire for several minutes.
That second yellow stripe marks the ones built to buy you time.
This bomb is blue. Blue means practice.
Not quite. Inside is a spotting charge, a puff of smoke that shows pilots where they hit.
In twenty nineteen, an A ten hit a bird and accidentally dropped three of them over northern Florida.
The Air Force's advice was simple. Don't approach it. Call it in.
A gray shell with a broken green stripe is the one you never want to see.
Gray means chemical. Dark green means toxic.
And when that green band is broken into dashes, it marks a binary nerve agent.
Two chemicals, stored apart, that only mix after the shell is fired.
The United States destroyed the last of its declared chemical weapons in twenty twenty-three.
